cards.title: Who translates?
cards.body:
You type **example.com** into your browser. But you learned in Module 2 that routers deliver packets using IP addresses, like `198.51.100.10`. They have no idea what "example.com" means.

People are good at remembering names and bad at remembering long numbers. Computers are the opposite. So before your browser can connect to example.com, something has to translate the name into an address. What does that?

cards.prompt: Why does the internet need a way to turn names into IP addresses?

options.text: Packets are delivered using IP addresses, but people find names easier to remember
Names make packets travel faster than numbers do
Names keep IP addresses secret from hackers
Websites don't have IP addresses, only names

cards.explanation: Every packet needs a destination **IP address**, because that's what routers use to deliver it. Names exist for people. Names don't change a packet's speed, and they don't hide anything: anyone can look up a website's address. Every website's server does have an IP address, and the name just points to it.

cards.title: The internet's phone book
cards.body:
Think of the contacts app on a phone. You tap a friend's **name**, and the phone looks up their **number** to make the call.

The internet has the same thing, called the **Domain Name System**, or **DNS**. You give it a name like `example.com`, and it gives back an IP address like `198.51.100.10`. That's called a **DNS lookup**.

A lookup happens before almost every connection you make: loading a website, sending a message, or starting a game.

cards.prompt: Match each part of the contacts-app idea to its internet version.
cards.explanation: The **name** is what people use, the **number** (IP address) is what the network uses, and **DNS** is the look-up service that connects the two. Once your device has the address, it can connect, just like a phone dials once it has the number.

cards.title: Reading a name from right to left
cards.body:
Domain names are read from **right to left**, from the most general part to the most specific. Take `www.example.com`:

- `com` is the **top-level domain**, or **TLD**: the last part of the name.
- `example` is the **domain** someone registered, so together it's `example.com`.
- `www` is a **subdomain**: a name the owner of example.com chose to add on the left.

There's even a hidden part: the **root**, written as a dot at the very end, `www.example.com.`. Browsers let you leave it off.

cards.prompt: Put the parts of `mail.example.org` in order, from the **most general** at the top to the **most specific** at the bottom.
cards.explanation: Read right to left: the **root** comes first, then the TLD `org`, then the domain `example` (making `example.org`), and finally the subdomain `mail`.

cards.prompt: In `shop.example.com`, which part is the **top-level domain**?
cards.explanation: The top-level domain is the **last** part: `com`. It's easy to pick `shop` because it comes first, but names are read from right to left. `shop` is a subdomain, and `example` is the registered domain.

cards.prompt: Time for a real lookup. Run `nslookup example.com` to ask DNS for example.com's address.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Ask DNS for the address of example.com
commands.output:
Server:		127.0.0.53
Address:	127.0.0.53#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:	example.com
Address: 198.51.100.10
Name:	example.com
Address: 2001:db8::10

cards.explanation:
DNS answered with **two** addresses for example.com: an IPv4 address, `198.51.100.10`, and an IPv6 address, `2001:db8::10`. Your device can use either one.

The `Server` lines at the top show who answered the question, and `#53` is a hint for Module 5. "Non-authoritative" means a helper server passed the answer on, rather than it coming straight from the server in charge of example.com's records. You'll meet both kinds of server in the next lesson.

Read from the right: the TLD is `org` and the registered domain is `example.org`. Everything to the left, including `login.example.com`, is just a subdomain that **example.org's owner** chose to add. It says "example.com" in the middle, but the owner of example.com has nothing to do with it. Tricksters use this to make links *look* like they belong to a site they don't.

cards.prompt: Some TLDs belong to countries. Two-letter TLDs are country codes, often from the country's own name (Germany is *Deutschland*). Match each TLD to what it stands for.

pairs.right: A general TLD anyone can register in

cards.explanation: Two-letter TLDs are **country codes**: `.uk` is the United Kingdom, `.jp` is Japan, and `.de` is Germany (*Deutschland* in German). Longer ones like `.com`, `.org` and `.net` are **generic** TLDs that aren't tied to one country.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Packets are delivered using **IP addresses**, but people prefer **names**.
- **DNS** (the Domain Name System) turns names into addresses, like a contacts app for the internet.
- Names are read **right to left**: the root, then the **TLD** (`com`), then the **domain** (`example`), then any **subdomain** (`www`).
- The owner of a domain controls every subdomain to its left.

Next: the journey a DNS question takes to find its answer.
